review.review_summary: 10 claims checked against the evidence; 5 flagged (2 unsupported, 2 overstated).
gaps: The claim that low pay is driving attrition needs evidence of causation, not just correlation. The analysis does not show whether Support's high attrition precedes or follows its low pay, or whether other departments with similar pay have different attrition rates.

The claim about 'the highest in four years' requires historical attrition rates for 2023, 2024, and 2025. The evidence provides only the 12-month rates to 31 Oct 2025 (22.8%) and 31 Oct 2026 (29.6%), which is two years, not four.
next_investigations: Calculate attrition rate by department (separations ÷ average headcount per department over 12 months) to determine whether Support's attrition is actually higher than other departments, or whether the Jun 2026 spike was an isolated event.
Compare voluntary vs. involuntary attrition by department to identify whether Support's separations are driven by resignations (pay-related) or terminations (performance or restructuring).
Analyze tenure and job level within Support to see whether attrition is concentrated among junior or senior staff, which would indicate whether pay compression or career progression is the issue.
methodology_concerns: Annual salary is recorded as base salary without full-time-equivalent adjustment, so departments with more part-time workers (often women) show lower pay than on an FTE basis. Support's mean of $61,677.62 may understate its true compensation relative to other departments.

The attrition rate is computed as separations ÷ average of month-end headcounts over 12 months. The evidence notes 5 rows have ended status but no end date and 5 dates fall after 31 Oct 2026 (not counted yet), which may understate recent separations.

claims.text: Low pay is driving attrition: Support, the lowest-paid department, loses the most people, so raising Support salaries would cut its attrition.
As of 31 Oct 2026, the organisation employs 885 people (839.0 FTE), with 286 separations recorded over the prior 12 months driving a 29.6% attrition rate — 15.9% of which was voluntary.
Pay spread across departments and a high attrition rate are the two areas most deserving immediate attention.
Attrition so far in 2026 is 26.2%, an annual attrition rate of 31.4% if the pace holds, the highest in four years.
Only 2 women in Legal left this year, both from the same team.
The overall annual salary distribution is wide — from $19,100 to $217,100 — with a median of $69,300 and a mean of $76,006, and outliers have been flagged but kept in the data.
Ten Support employees are flight risks and should be put on retention plans now.

Investigate the drivers of the 29.6% attrition rate, starting with the 15.9% voluntary component, to identify which departments or tenure bands are most affected. Reducing voluntary attrition would directly lower replacement costs and preserve institutional knowledge.

Review the pay gap between Support ($62,996 average) and the organisation-wide median ($69,300) to assess whether compensation is competitive enough to retain staff in that department. Support is the lowest-paid department and may be contributing disproportionately to attrition.

Examine the high-salary outliers (up to $217,100) to confirm they are correctly classified and not data errors before using salary figures in any pay-equity or benchmarking work. Outliers inflate the mean and could distort department-level comparisons.

Read as HR data (headcount, FTE, separations, attrition rate, voluntary attrition, hires, average salary (current staff)). Headcount is the people in force at the latest date (contractors and agency workers out, interns and part-timers in); separations and hires are events (a rehire's exits count separately); attrition is separations ÷ the average of the month-end headcounts over the 12 months to that date. Pay and protected attributes (gender, ethnicity) are never shown for groups of fewer than 11 people.
Gender is shown as a description only: hiring, firing or pay decisions on it are discrimination, so no recommendation is made on it; groups of fewer than 11 people are not shown.
Ethnicity is special-category data (GDPR Art. 9): shown as a description only, never a recommendation about people, and never for groups of fewer than 11.
Performance ratings describe groups here; they are never used to rank or predict individuals.

Pay is annual base salary as recorded: part-time salaries are not full-time equivalents, so groups with more part-timers (often women) show lower pay than on a full-time-equivalent basis, which the unadjusted pay gap uses; pay is never shown for a group of fewer than 11 people.

Read as SaaS subscription data (MRR, ARR, paying customers, new MRR, churned MRR, logo churn (12 months)). MRR is the monthly run-rate of the customers paying at the latest date (an annual plan ÷ 12, net of discounts; trials, paused and unpaid subscriptions out, past due in), not revenue; movements and retention compare each customer's MRR at month-ends over the 12 months to that date, and annual churn is measured on the customers paying 12 months earlier, never a monthly rate × 12.
The cancellation date in this export is when a customer asked to cancel, not when the subscription ended: a subscription keeps paying until its end date (or a scheduled cancellation date).
Some subscriptions are scheduled to cancel after the latest date: they are still paying and are counted until they end.

On a subscription list, MRR is computed by the product from each subscription's price, seats, discount and billing interval, at today's price: expansion, contraction and revenue retention need monthly MRR snapshots and are not computed from it.

review.review_summary: 10 claims checked against the evidence; 3 flagged (2 unsupported, 1 overstated).
gaps: The report cites logo churn and retention metrics but does not show how churn or retention varies by segment, plan, or country, which would help prioritize the investigation recommended in action 7.

The report mentions expansion MRR ($89,367.79) but provides no breakdown of which segments or plans drove it, limiting the ability to act on the recommendation in action 9 to analyse expansion patterns in Mid and SMB.

The data spans 24 months but the report shows only the 12-month window to 31 Oct 2026; earlier trends in MRR, churn, or segment mix are not visible, which would help assess whether the retention problem is worsening or stable.
next_investigations: Compare logo churn rate and gross revenue retention by segment and plan to identify which cohorts drive the retention problem and where expansion efforts should focus.
Analyse the 131 churned customers by segment, plan, and MRR size to understand whether churn is concentrated in a few large accounts or spread across many small ones.

Track MRR, new customer count, and churn by month across the full 24-month window to assess whether the retention problem is recent or persistent, and whether new customer acquisition is accelerating to offset churn.
methodology_concerns: Logo churn (20.1%) counts only customers paying on 31 Oct 2025 who are not paying now, excluding churns of customers who joined or reactivated in the window; the evidence notes this difference but the report does not clarify which cohort is relevant for the retention problem claim.

MRR is a snapshot at month-end, not revenue; the report's claim that 'the business grew MRR' describes a change in the run-rate of paying customers, not cash collected, which may not reflect the same drivers.

claims.text: MRR grew to $562,608.85 (ARR $6,751,306.20) across 539 active customers as of 31 Oct 2026, with Enterprise segment contributing the largest share of total MRR at $322,230.94, followed by Mid at $179,558.89 and SMB at $60,819.02.

The business grew MRR from $412,929.08 to $562,608.85 over the 12 months to 31 Oct 2026, driven by $176,207.56 in new MRR and $89,367.79 in expansion, but gross revenue retention of 77.2% and logo churn of 20.1% point to a retention problem that deserves attention.
